item.title: On Unserious Thinking
item.description: Expecting b2c agents to take over commerce feels unserious.
item.content:encoded:
I.

Expecting b2c agents to take over commerce feels unserious. Businesses will protect their margins with their own agents or block outside ones.

II.

Consider ecommerce, all the rage these days with agents like Muse and Instinct. On its Q3 2026 earnings call Meta reported over 10m Muse setups in the US and Canada with about 25% active daily. Over a quarter of weekly users used it for shopping with average purchases above $200, including travel.

Let’s assume:

  • Twice as many weekly users as daily users: 2.5m daily → 5m weekly.
  • A quarter of those weekly users buy once a month at $200: $3bn in annual purchases.
  • A 5% total take: roughly 3% for card processing including interchange plus 2% for the agent → $150m in annual gross fees.

ChatGPT doubled weekly users in roughly nine months. The dashed line applies that pace to the same assumed 5m starting point:

III.

In year three:

  • Bear, roughly pre-IPO Duolingo pace (20% annual growth in monthly users): 10m weekly users × 25% buying monthly → $300m annual gross fees.
  • Base, roughly early Snapchat pace (daily users roughly doubling in a year): 50m weekly users × 25% buying monthly → $1.5bn annual gross fees.
  • Bull, roughly ChatGPT pace (weekly users grew from 200m to nearly 700m in a year): 200m weekly users × 50% buying twice monthly → $24bn annual gross fees.

The bull case requires $480bn in annual purchases, or $4,800 per shopper. Let’s even let Muse keep the entire 5%, including the processing share, and assume zero costs:

Annual figures Muse bull case, year three Meta Family of Apps, 2025 actuals
Revenue $24bn $198.8bn
Operating profit $24bn $102.5bn
Operating margin 100% assumed 51.6% actual

IV.

Self-discovery can subsidize the price paid by the customer through advertising. I expect businesses to use agents to improve algorithmically targeted performance ads and keep the eyeballs viewing them.

Consider Amazon’s advertising business and Meta’s own ad business. These totals include brand and video ads too:

Revenue / increase
Muse bull case, year three (5% total take) $24bn
Amazon ad revenue increase, 2025 vs. 2024 $12.4bn
Amazon total ad revenue, 2025 $68.6bn
Meta ad revenue increase, 2025 vs. 2024 $35.5bn
Meta total ad revenue, 2025 $196.2bn

A 12.2% lift in Meta’s ad revenue would add about $24bn a year, matching Muse’s bull case. If advertiser spending rises proportionally with conversion, that could mean going from a 2% conversion rate to about 2.24%. Meta probably gets more from its constrained inference capacity by improving ad targeting than by putting it into Muse.

V.

Consumer productivity agents feel like a shortsighted grasp at use cases to me. Travel makes sense when people already have a destination and dates and want help booking. Beyond that I struggle to see the case for an independent agent operating on top of the existing ecommerce ecosystem.

Digital performance advertising may be the best business model ever. Amazon has already blocked Muse and sued to stop Perplexity’s Comet from shopping on its site. It handles an estimated 39.7% of US retail ecommerce sales in 2026. It’s hard to square the expected success of independent shopping agents with a retailer that large already blocking them.

item.title: Small Talk
item.description: It was a sticky Thursday afternoon.
item.content:encoded:
I.

It was a sticky Thursday afternoon. The air wrapped around and between the leaves while the boys watched cars grind north on Third Avenue.

II.

Steve tapped his black shoes together. “I’m hungry.”

“Yeah, it was a lousy lunch. Those sandwiches were like the ones from soccer.”

Steve nodded.

“I’ll make you something tonight, maybe tortellini.”

Steve smiled and closed his eyes. “So where’s Mom now?”

Elliott shook his head. “I don’t know.”

Steve turned towards the tall oak doors. “She never liked this place.”

“Yeah, she said it was better to sleep in the morning. Remember that science study thing? The one in our group chat only with Mo–?”

On the sidewalk to their right, a bit closer to the park than the Avenue, water and glass, cut flowers from a vase, white and pink, a kind man, his cheek pressed into pavement, above, a girl and a balcony rail. A scream.

“Did she drop that?”

“Had to… look at all… I don’t… Stevey, he’s not moving,” Elliott whispered.

Someone ran across the street. Faces followed and a delivery worker shook the man and a different man stabbed at his phone. Steve watched the concrete stain.

There were sirens and flashes and uniforms. Elliott sank back into the shade. Steve listened to the traffic and the girl and her elbow slipped inside.

III.

A man approached, not the priest.

He stopped at their feet. “It’s time to carry your mom outside.” Steve got up first and rubbed his eyes.
